short_description: A textbook that develops Bayesian reasoning, statistical learning and deep learning as one probabilistic framework, from Bayes' rule and decision theory to neural networks, transformers and AI agents, with code in R and Python.
description:
Modern AI rests on one principle: learning from data under uncertainty. This book builds that principle from the ground up, from Bayes' rule and decision theory to the transformers behind today's large language models.

Three parts follow the way the ideas developed. Bayesian learning covers probability, utility and decisions, A/B testing, hypothesis testing, stochastic processes, Gaussian processes and reinforcement learning. Statistical learning covers data and pattern matching, regression, logistic regression, tree models, forecasting and model selection. Deep learning covers neural networks, stochastic gradient descent, convolutional networks, language models and AI agents. Worked examples come from finance, sports, medicine, marketing and operations, with code in R and Python and exercises at the end of every chapter.

Unlike treatments that present machine learning as a toolbox of algorithms, this book treats uncertainty as a first class concern and shows how linear regression, logistic regression and neural networks sit inside one probabilistic framework. Readers learn to quantify what a model does not know, to turn a prediction into a decision, and to see why large language models hallucinate.

The book grew out of courses the authors teach to MBA students at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business and to engineering students at George Mason University. It assumes introductory statistics and high school calculus and suits graduate students, data scientists and practitioners who want the mathematics behind the methods.

chapters.title: Probability and Uncertainty
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks how uncertainty is measured and which rules probabilities must obey. It presents probability as a degree of belief revealed by betting odds, and argues through the Dutch book that coherence (no sure loss) implies the rules of finitely additive probability and conditional probability, derived in an appendix with payoff matrices and determinants. It then covers odds, random variables, mass, density and cumulative distribution functions, the inverse CDF method, change of variables, expectation, variance, covariance, correlation, portfolio variance, the weak law of large numbers (proved under finite variance with Chebyshev's inequality), the strong law and the ergodic theorem (stated), the Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson and normal distributions, joint, marginal and conditional distributions, and independence. Examples include exacta betting, the birthday problem, confounding in batting averages, and a normal model for the 1987 crash.

the betting definition of subjective probability (Ramsey 1926; de Finetti 1937); Dutch book coherence as the basis of finitely additive probability (Ramsey 1926; de Finetti 1937; Shimony 1955); the axioms of probability (Kolmogorov 1933); the frequency definition through collectives (von Mises), criticized by Ville 1939; the weak law of large numbers (Jakob Bernoulli 1713, generalized by Poisson 1837 and Chebyshev 1867); the strong law for Bernoulli trials (Borel 1909); the strong law under a variance condition (Kolmogorov 1933); methods for studying coincidences, applied to the birthday problem (Diaconis and Mosteller 1989); the Harville formula for exacta bets (named in the chapter, no reference); the three coin paradox (Galton 1894, essay linked in the chapter); subjective expected utility (Savage, building on von Neumann and Morgenstern).

chapters.title: Bayes' Rule
chapters.summary:
How should probabilities be revised when new evidence arrives? The chapter develops Bayes' rule (Bayes' theorem) for conditional probability, turning a prior probability and a likelihood into a posterior probability, with sequential updating, conditional independence, the law of total probability and the odds form with the Bayes factor. Worked examples include base rate neglect, craps, the Monty Hall problem, the search for the submarine USS Scorpion, Wald and damage to returning aircraft, the prosecutor's fallacy, the island problem, Cromwell's rule, Hume on miracles, the Sally Clark case, the O. J. Simpson case, and the chess cheating accusation against Nakamura. It then treats the naive Bayes classifier, sensitivity, specificity, type I and type II errors, positive predictive value, Monte Carlo simulation of the 2012 US presidential election with a Dirichlet distribution, and Bayesian networks with explaining away.

chapters.title: Bayesian Learning
chapters.summary:
How does one learn about an unknown parameter from data and predict new observations using Bayes' rule? The chapter develops Bayesian parameter learning: prior, likelihood, posterior, marginal likelihood, posterior predictive distribution and sequential updating. It motivates the approach with exchangeability, de Finetti's representation theorem, subjective probability elicited by betting and the Dutch book argument. It introduces sufficient statistics and conjugate priors and gives closed form posteriors for the Beta Binomial model (Black Swan problem, Thompson sampling for clinical trials, shrinkage of batting averages), the Poisson Gamma model (count data, Poisson and Cox processes, Peso problem), the Exponential Gamma model, the Normal model with unknown mean, with unknown variance (inverse gamma prior) and with both unknown (Normal Gamma), the multivariate Normal, and mixtures of conjugate priors. It derives the Normal posterior by completing the square. Examples use English Premier League scores, stock returns and an American football point spread. The final section bridges to computation: posterior consistency, Monte Carlo integration, Markov chain Monte Carlo, detailed balance for the Metropolis rule, the Gibbs sampler and posterior predictive simulation.

chapters.title: Utility, Risk and Decisions
chapters.summary:
The chapter asks how an agent should choose actions under uncertainty and how a posterior distribution becomes a decision. It presents expected utility theory, its axioms and the uniqueness of utility up to positive affine transformation, risk aversion, certainty equivalents, risk premium and constant relative risk aversion (CRRA), and the Kelly criterion for growth optimal betting with a leveraged Berkshire Hathaway example. A historical section treats de Finetti's reinsurance retention problem, Markowitz mean variance portfolios, Bellman's principle of optimality and Livermore's trading maxims. Statistical decision theory covers loss functions, classical risk, Bayes risk, minimax rules, posterior expected loss and generalized Bayes rules. Paradoxes and puzzles include Saint Petersburg, Newcomb, Ellsberg, Allais, the winner's curse, lemons and two envelopes, with decision trees for medical testing and a mudslide wall. The chapter ends with Nash equilibrium, mixed strategies and tit for tat in a marble game.

#### New results

The catalog records two informal results cited to earlier papers of Polson and coauthors: Livermore's maxims as Bellman value comparisons (Polson and Witte 2014) and the option value of learning in Bernoulli Beta asset allocation (Jacquier and Polson 2013).

- [Option value of learning in Bernoulli Beta asset allocation](https://vsokolov.org/books/bayes_ai_deep_learning/results.html#bernoulli_beta_option_value_of_learning) (Section 4.2.3, page 162; conditional on the dynamic Bellman solution of Jacquier and Polson (2013), which the chapter quotes and does not derive; the utility function, the payoff structure and the recursion behind the 11.7 percent allocation are not specified): With a Beta prior on an unknown success probability and unfavorable prior odds, the myopic Kelly rule invests nothing while the dynamic Bellman solution invests a small positive amount because of the option value of learning. chapters.title: A/B Testing
chapters.summary:
How do we decide whether the difference between two variants, such as two web page designs, is real or only sampling noise? The chapter presents the classical frequentist toolkit for A/B testing and randomized experiments. It derives the variance of a sample mean of uncorrelated observations, defines the standard error, illustrates the central limit theorem by simulation, and develops confidence intervals, null and alternative hypotheses, the p value, the significance level, Type I and Type II errors, the z score and a five step testing procedure. Worked R examples include the Trial of the Pyx, the Mythbusters yawning experiment, Coke versus Pepsi, Avonex, Viagra, Lord Rayleigh's argon data, SimCity and Google search algorithms, with tests for proportions and a two sample t test. It then treats multiple testing, the Bonferroni correction and the false discovery rate, and discusses randomized controlled trials, field experiments, split plot designs, causation and observational data. Bayesian testing is deferred to a later chapter.

#### From the literature

the central limit theorem and its origin in the De Moivre Laplace theorem (de Moivre 1738); the Galton board (Galton 1889); the Benjamini Hochberg procedure for the false discovery rate (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995); the 1948 streptomycin trial in tuberculosis, attributed by the chapter to Austin Bradford Hill; randomization, experimental design and split plot designs (Ronald Fisher and colleagues at Rothamsted); the discovery of argon (Lord Rayleigh); the five sigma criterion in the Higgs boson announcement (two teams at CERN); a diet and mammographic density study (Garcia Arenzana and coauthors 2014); a randomized field experiment on electoral fraud in Russia (Enikolopov, Korovkin, Petrova, Sonin and Zakharov 2013); a randomized experiment on environmental audits in Gujarat (Duflo, Greenstone, Pande and Ryan 2013).

chapters.title: Bayesian Hypothesis Testing
chapters.summary:
How does a Bayesian decide between a null and an alternative hypothesis, and how does that compare with p values and Neyman Pearson tests? The chapter covers errors, size and power, the likelihood principle, posterior odds and Bayes factors for sharp and composite hypotheses, and decisions by expected loss. It derives the Bayes factor for a normal mean, defines credible and highest posterior density (HPD) sets, and proves that an HPD set is smallest among sets of equal posterior probability. It treats sequential analysis, clinical trial design, and multi armed bandit experiments with Thompson sampling. It closes with Lindley's paradox, a Neyman Pearson paradox, lower bounds on the posterior probability of a point null over classes of priors, Jeffreys' decision rule, and Cromwell's rule.

chapters.title: Stochastic Processes
chapters.summary:
The chapter introduces stochastic processes as distributions over functions from an index set to a state space, with the Markov property, and develops Brownian motion (the Wiener process) and the Poisson process as building blocks of continuous time models. For geometric Brownian motion it derives the mean and variance of a price at a horizon and states the Merton rule, the continuous time analog of the Kelly criterion. Sports betting examples define implied volatility: a Brownian motion model of the score difference gives win probabilities and a time varying implied volatility for Super Bowl XLVII, and a Skellam process calibrated to bookmaker odds does the same for an English Premier League match. It states the Lévy Itô decomposition and presents stochastic volatility models with jumps (SV, SVJ, SVCJ, SVIJ) with Bayesian MCMC inference.

chapters.title: Gaussian Processes
chapters.summary:
How can a prior be placed directly on an unknown function, updated with observations, and used to report uncertainty at every input? The chapter introduces the Gaussian process (GP), a collection of random variables any finite number of which have a joint Gaussian distribution, specified by a mean function and a covariance (kernel) function and written $f \sim \mathcal{GP}(m, k)$. It uses the zero mean squared exponential kernel (radial basis function, RBF) with signal variance and length scale hyperparameters, and draws sample paths from the prior with mvrnorm in R. It states the closed form posterior mean and covariance of GP regression, obtained by conditioning a multivariate normal vector on noiseless observations, and applies them to the sine function. Hyperparameters are estimated by maximizing the log marginal likelihood (maximum likelihood estimation, MLE), which the chapter reads as an Occam's razor balance between data fit and a log determinant complexity penalty. The chapter states the gradient for the squared exponential kernel, passes it to BFGS through optim, compares the result with the laGP package, and fits the motorcycle accident data (mcycle in the R package MASS), with wider uncertainty where observations are few. Exercises cover kernel ridge regression and the Matern kernel.

#### From the literature

the laGP package, developed by Bobby Gramacy, for estimating Gaussian process hyperparameters and approximate inference on large data sets; the closed form conditioning of a multivariate normal vector that yields the GP posterior mean and covariance, described as a standard property of the multivariate normal distribution, with a reference to Rasmussen and Williams (2006), Appendix A.2. The chapter gives no authors or years for the squared exponential kernel, jitter or BFGS.

#### New results

chapters.title: Reinforcement Learning
chapters.summary:
How should an agent choose which data to collect, or which action to take, when each choice changes what it learns and earns next? The chapter treats sequential experimental design and sequential decision making under uncertainty. It covers multi armed bandit experiments (Thompson sampling with Beta posteriors, the posterior probability that an arm is best, a regret based stopping rule, contextual bandits), the Bellman principle of optimality and its use to derive the 37% rule for the secretary problem, checked by Monte Carlo simulation, and Markov decision processes (state value and action value functions, the Bellman expectation equation solved by a matrix inverse, the Bellman optimality equation solved by policy iteration and value iteration, with student chain, forest management, maze and Deal or No Deal examples). It then presents model free methods (Monte Carlo prediction with first visit and every visit averaging, epsilon greedy exploration, temporal difference learning, Q learning) and Bayesian optimization with a Gaussian process surrogate and the expected improvement acquisition function, whose closed form is derived and applied to a taxi fleet simulator.

chapters.title: Unreasonable Effectiveness of Data
chapters.summary:
This chapter opens Part II and asks when aggregating many observations or judgments yields accurate prediction, and when it entrenches error. It begins with the history of data driven estimation: the meridian arc data of Boscovich and a linear regression of arc length on the squared sine of latitude to find the shape of the Earth, the average of pairwise slopes, least absolute deviations, least squares, the weighted median and regression to the mean. A Formula One example shows real time strategy optimization from sensor data. The second half studies the wisdom and madness of crowds: speculative bubbles, Galton's ox weight contest, where the median of about 800 guesses fell within 1 percent of the true weight, and the smart money and dumb money model of learning one's type from prices as an identification problem with posterior odds and a likelihood ratio. It names the conditions that made Galton's crowd wise (independence, diversity, incentive alignment, appropriate aggregation) and draws lessons for ensemble methods, the bias variance tradeoff, calibration, feedback loops and prediction markets.

chapters.title: Pattern Matching
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks how a prediction rule is learned from data and how its accuracy is judged. It treats supervised learning as finding a map $y = f(x)$ from a training dataset, and separates classification, regression and ranking. It contrasts the mean rule and the nearest neighbor rule as the two ends of the bias variance trade off, then parametric and nonparametric models, and traditional models (linear regression, generalized linear and additive models, principal component regression) with deep learning as a composition of layers instead of a sum of functions. Estimation is developed through the likelihood: maximum likelihood, the negative log likelihood as a loss, least squares derived from a normal model, the logistic function for Bernoulli responses, penalized likelihood and regularization, and the Bayesian posterior with its maximum a posteriori estimate. Predictive performance is assessed with train test splits, cross validation, MSE, MAE, precision, recall, F1 score and the confusion matrix, with an argument against R squared.

#### From the literature

chapters.title: Linear Regression
chapters.summary:
How can an output be predicted from inputs with a model linear in its parameters, and how certain are the estimated coefficients? The chapter covers least squares: the model $y = X\beta + \epsilon$, basis functions, the normal equations $X^\top y = X^\top X \beta$ and their closed form solution, and fitting with the R function lm. It derives the mean and covariance of the least squares estimator, argues that it is normally distributed under independent normal errors with constant variance, and uses this for standard errors, t statistics, p values, confidence and prediction intervals, residuals, outliers, influential points and regression to the mean. Examples cover house prices, stock and portfolio return regressions including the Capital Asset Pricing Model (Keynes, Google, Yahoo!), log and log log transformations, power laws, price elasticity, interactions, dummy variables, and golf earnings. It shows that the median minimizes the sum of absolute deviations, presents the quantile loss, and mentions the Huber loss. It ends with Bayesian linear regression: a Gaussian prior, the conjugate Gaussian posterior, ridge and lasso as Gaussian and Laplace priors, and a pointer to the horseshoe prior.

chapters.title: Logistic Regression and Generalized Linear Models
chapters.summary:
How do we model and assess a binary or multiclass outcome from inputs? The chapter develops logistic regression from a binomial (Bernoulli) likelihood and the logistic function, fitted by maximum likelihood (cross entropy loss, BFGS), with softmax and logits for several classes, log odds interpretation of coefficients, and the probit alternative. Examples use NBA point spreads, tennis match statistics, Hong Kong horse racing and a LinkedIn study of executive careers. Evaluation topics are thresholds, accuracy, the confusion matrix, the ROC curve, AUC, confounding, expected profit and imbalanced data (F1 score, SMOTE). It explains the kernel trick through the Gram matrix, then generalized linear models: link functions, Poisson and Gamma regression, deviance, and likelihood ratio comparison of nested models. It ends with Bayesian logistic regression by Polya Gamma data augmentation and a Gibbs sampler, stated without proof, with an R implementation using the BayesLogit package and a horse race betting application.

chapters.title: Tree Models
chapters.summary:
How can nested if then rules predict a response, how can trees be combined to cut variance, and how can tree ensembles estimate causal effects from observational data? The chapter builds regression trees by greedy recursive binary splitting (CART), prunes them by cost complexity pruning, and builds classification trees that split by the Gini index or cross entropy. It presents bagging, random forests and gradient boosting. A long section applies Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) to causal inference, covering potential outcomes, ATE, ATT and CATE, SUTVA, ignorability, positivity, regularization priors, Bayesian backfitting MCMC and counterfactual posterior draws, with the Lalonde job training data compared against propensity score matching. An appendix covers the 1/N variance rule, the curse of dimensionality, trees as adaptive nearest neighbors, equal weights for exchangeable predictors, and a Chebyshev bound relating ensemble error to margin and covariance between trees.

chapters.title: Forecasting
chapters.summary:
How can time series be forecast with Bayesian state space models, and how do such forecasts compare with machine learning forecasters? The chapter builds structural time series models (local level, local linear and semilocal linear trend, seasonal and regression components) from an observation equation and a transition equation, fitted by Markov chain Monte Carlo with the bsts R package. Examples are nowcasting weekly initial claims for unemployment insurance from Google search data with spike and slab variable selection, long term forecasting of the S&P 500 index, and dynamic logistic regression for recession probabilities. It then describes quantile regression forests and the temporal fusion transformer, with a benchmark against bsts. An optional section derives the Kalman filter recursions and presents the forward filtering backward sampling algorithm, forward backward recursions for hidden Markov models, regime switching and changepoint models. The chapter closes with particle learning for general mixtures and a Poisson mixture example.

chapters.title: Model Selection
chapters.summary:
How should a predictive model be chosen without fitting noise? The chapter covers overfitting and underfitting, prediction versus interpretation (Breiman's two cultures), Q Q plots, the Runge function, and the bias variance decomposition of squared error, which it derives. chapters.title: Statistical Learning Theory and Regularization
chapters.summary:
How does shrinkage reduce estimation risk in high dimensions, and why is regularization the same as choosing a prior? The chapter starts from the normal means problem and presents Stein's paradox: the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) of a multivariate normal mean has constant risk and is inadmissible under squared error loss in dimension three or more. It covers the James Stein estimator and its empirical Bayes interpretation, the bias variance decomposition and sparse signal recovery. Its main theme is maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation, where the penalty is a negative log prior. Ridge regression (Gaussian prior), the Lasso (Laplace prior), the bridge estimator (exponential power prior), the horseshoe prior, spike and slab priors and L0 subset selection (single best replacement algorithm) are developed in this frame, with scale mixture representations and proximal operators. Examples use baseball batting averages, firm performance screening and traffic speed filtering.

chapters.title: Neural Networks
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks how deep learning extends generalized linear models and what hidden layers add to regression and classification. A feedforward neural network is a composition of layers, each an affine map followed by a nonlinear activation function; wide and shallow models are contrasted with deep and narrow networks that learn features. Products and maxima are written through univariate functions of linear combinations, and nested ReLU layers reduce to a max sum network. R examples separate an inner cluster from an outer ring with a hand specified hidden layer and fit one hidden layer networks by BFGS to noisy quadratic and interaction data. The chapter then covers activation functions, vanishing gradients, autoencoders, transfer learning, mixture of experts and ensembles. It proves no theorems.

chapters.title: Theory of Deep Learning
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks what the approximation of multivariate functions says about deep learning. It defines ridge functions and projection pursuit regression, states the Kolmogorov superposition theorem (KST) with the history of its constructive proofs, and describes Kolmogorov Arnold networks and the Kolmogorov generalized additive model (K GAM), a two layer network with fixed inner features and learned outer functions. It compares ReLU partitions of input space with CART trees and reads kernel smoothing, nearest neighbors and transformer attention as kernel estimators. Deep learning is framed as representation learning, with PCA and partial least squares as linear baselines, and double descent is illustrated by polynomial regression. The chapter closes with minimax, posterior concentration and deep learner convergence rates, including a dimension free rate for generalized additive models. Most results are cited rather than proved.

chapters.title: Gradient Descent
chapters.summary:
How are the parameters of a model with millions of weights fitted when second order methods such as Newton's method and BFGS are too costly? The chapter treats estimation as minimizing a negative log likelihood and develops first order methods. It covers gradient descent and the learning rate, with least squares and logistic regression fitted on the iris data and compared with lm and glm, and stochastic gradient descent with mini batches. It traces backpropagation from the perceptron and the delta rule, and explains automatic differentiation in forward mode and reverse mode with dual numbers, a computational graph and a JAX example. It surveys momentum, Nesterov acceleration, AdaGrad, RMSprop and Adam, states the Robbins Monro stochastic approximation algorithm and its step size conditions, and presents the EM, ECM and ECME algorithms and simulated annealing.

chapters.title: Quantile Neural Networks
chapters.summary:
How can posteriors, predictive distributions and expected utilities be learned directly, without density estimation or an explicit likelihood? The chapter introduces quantile neural networks, which represent a conditional distribution by its quantile function and are trained with the check (pinball) loss. It opens with an inventory decision in which asymmetric costs select a quantile, then covers linear quantile regression on the mtcars data, a network that takes the quantile level as an input, a cosine embedding of that level, noncrossing constraints, a synthetic comparison of an implicit and an explicit network, and the 1 Wasserstein distance. Demand forecasting (a linear quantile baseline on simulated data, with a coverage check) follows. The chapter then turns to Bayesian inference: a generative formulation through noise outsourcing, Bayes' rule for quantiles with a normal normal example as a Wang distortion, and maximum expected utility as an integral over the quantile level, checked on a portfolio problem with exponential utility against its closed form. It closes with an optional comparison with quantile trend filtering, distributional reinforcement learning and practical checks for a learned quantile network.

chapters.title: Convolutional Neural Networks
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks how a neural network for image data can use the spatial structure of images, and how a convolutional neural network (CNN) compares with a fully connected network on handwritten digits. It starts from two priors, locality and translation equivariance, and from the history of the Neocognitron. A filter (kernel) is a small matrix of weights shared across positions. A hand calculation of a diagonal filter on $3\times3$ patches of a $5\times5$ cross yields responses 3 and 1, and shifting a stroke one pixel moves the response, which is translation equivariance, whereas invariance would leave the output unchanged. The chapter defines stride, receptive field and same and valid padding, notes that deep learning libraries compute cross correlation and call it convolution, and applies a moving average filter of length 10 to a noisy sine wave. A toy example with two fixed $3\times3$ filters, a global maximum and a softmax layer separates cross, diagonal and right diagonal images, and global pooling discards position. On MNIST (28 by 28 grayscale digits, ten classes), a fully connected JAX network (784, 1024, 1024 and 10 units, tanh, log softmax, minibatch SGD) reaches 80 percent training and 77 percent held out accuracy. A PyTorch CNN (two Conv2d layers, ReLU, 2 by 2 max pooling, two linear layers, Adadelta) reaches 93 percent, with 1,199,882 parameters against 1,863,690. Most CNN parameters sit in its dense head, and the chapter warns that the gap does not isolate convolution, since architecture, activation, optimizer and framework all differ. The chapter develops intuition and code; it states no theorems.

the Neocognitron, a hierarchical network with convolutional and pooling layers inspired by simple and complex cells of the visual cortex (Fukushima 1980; Hubel and Wiesel are named without a reference); backpropagation applied to a simplified Neocognitron for alphabet recognition (Zhang, Itoh, Tanida and Ichioka 1988)

chapters.title: Natural Language Processing
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks how discrete text can be turned into vectors a neural network can use, and how attention and the Transformer produce context dependent representations of language. It starts with one hot encoding, Twenty Questions and the distributional hypothesis. Word2vec (skip gram and continuous bag of words, CBOW) is followed by two remedies for the cost of the softmax, negative sampling and hierarchical softmax, then by GloVe as weighted matrix factorization of log co occurrence counts, a War and Peace example, and subword tokenization by FastText n grams and byte pair encoding (BPE). Attention is developed from queries, keys and values and from kernel smoothing (Nadaraya Watson regression), then as self attention over a sequence, multi head attention, and sinusoidal positional encodings. The Transformer is an encoder decoder stack with masked decoding, feed forward layers, residual connections and layer normalization, followed by the encoder only, decoder only and encoder decoder families. BERT is a historical case study (masked language modeling, next sentence prediction, ELMo and GPT). Transfer learning covers a sentiment decision, natural language inference, named entity recognition and extractive question answering, and compression covers knowledge distillation. The chapter closes with theoretical limits. It states known results without proof and develops no new theorem.

chapters.title: AI Agents
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks what changes when the output of a large language model is allowed to act, and how such agents are built, orchestrated, evaluated and kept safe. An LLM agent combines perception, reasoning, memory (retrieval augmented generation) and tools reached by function calling, driven by an orchestrator in a reason act observe loop. The chapter surveys ReAct, orchestration patterns (sequential, parallel, hierarchical, dynamic) for multi agent systems, agent evaluation and benchmarks (SWE bench, TAU bench, WebArena, ALFRED), agent safety (prompt injection, goal misalignment, corrigibility, red teaming) and embodied agents (sensor fusion, the sim to real gap, vision language action models). Case studies cover a Replit agent that destroyed production data, Anthropic's AI Safety Level 3 protections, ChatDev and a red teaming project. The text states no theorems and has no code; R exercises build an agent loop, simulate agent costs and score a rule based red team scanner.

#### From the literature

ChatDev, communicative agents for software development with chat chains (Qian et al. 2024); personality, values and demographics of GPT 3 (Miotto, Rossberg and Kleinberg 2022); a psychometric framework for evaluating and shaping personality in language models with the IPIP NEO and Big Five Inventory (Serapio García et al. 2025); generative agent simulations of 1,000 people built from two hour interviews (Park et al. 2024); the ReAct reason plus act framework (Google); AI Safety Level 3 protections with Constitutional Classifiers, activated for Claude Opus 4 in May 2025 (Anthropic); a red teaming study of a computer use agent with over 1,200 test scenarios (Toloka); the July 2025 Replit agent incident (reported by The Register); Shakey the Robot (SRI International, 1960s); Gemini Robotics, a vision language action model built on Gemini 2.0, and the ASIMOV safety dataset (Google DeepMind).

results.name: Posterior probability that Nakamura did not cheat given a 45 win streak
results.status_text: conditional on prior odds of innocence N = 10000, the assessment attributed to Viswanathan Anand (N = 500 in the sensitivity analysis), a streak of 45 wins in 46 games with a draw counted as not a win, independent games with one common win probability q = 0.8916 (Nakamura's own estimate), and probability 1 of the evidence under guilt
results.conditions: prior odds of innocence N = 10000, the assessment attributed to Viswanathan Anand (N = 500 in the sensitivity analysis), a streak of 45 wins in 46 games with a draw counted as not a win, independent games with one common win probability q = 0.8916 (Nakamura's own estimate), and probability 1 of the evidence under guilt
results.origin_text: First stated in Maharaj, Polson and Sokolov (2023), Kramnik vs Nakamura or Bayes vs P Value, SSRN 4648621.
results.summary: Under Anand's prior of 1 in 10000 and a binomial model of the streak, the posterior probability that Nakamura did not cheat is 0.9965.
results.statement: Let $I$ be innocence (no cheating), $G$ guilt, and $E$ the evidence, a streak of 45 wins in 46 games. Suppose the prior odds of innocence are $O(I) = P(I)/P(G) = N$, that $P(E\mid G) = 1$, and that $P(E\mid I) = p = \binom{46}{45} q^{45}(1-q)$ with per game win probability $q = 0.8916$ (the chapter reports $p = 0.029$, rounded). Then the Bayes factor in favor of innocence is $P(E\mid I)/P(E\mid G) = p$, the posterior odds of innocence are $O(I\mid E) = Np$, and $P(I\mid E) = Np/(Np+1)$. For $N = 10000$ the posterior odds of innocence are $285$, $P(G\mid E) = 0.003492$ and $P(I\mid E) = 0.9965$. For $N = 500$, $P(I\mid E) = 0.9345$.
results.label: exm-nakamura

results.name: Option value of learning in Bernoulli Beta asset allocation
results.status_text: conditional on the dynamic Bellman solution of Jacquier and Polson (2013), which the chapter quotes and does not derive; the utility function, the payoff structure and the recursion behind the 11.7 percent allocation are not specified
results.conditions: the dynamic Bellman solution of Jacquier and Polson (2013), which the chapter quotes and does not derive; the utility function, the payoff structure and the recursion behind the 11.7 percent allocation are not specified
results.origin_text: First stated in Jacquier and Polson (2013), Asset Allocation in Finance: A Bayesian Perspective, in Bayesian Theory and Applications, Oxford University Press, pages 501 to 515.
results.summary: With a Beta prior on an unknown success probability and unfavorable prior odds, the myopic Kelly rule invests nothing while the dynamic Bellman solution invests a small positive amount because of the option value of learning.
results.statement: Consider a sequence of bets with unknown success probability $p$ and prior $p \sim \mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)$. If $\alpha < \beta$ (unfavorable prior odds), the myopic Kelly rule invests nothing, whereas the dynamic Bellman solution invests a small positive amount even for a risk averse investor, because investing yields information that may reveal that the true environment is favorable (the option value of learning). For example, with the uniform prior $\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)$, 10 remaining periods and one observed failure (posterior $\mathrm{Beta}(1,2)$, expected odds 1:2 against), an investor might optimally allocate 11.7 percent.
results.label: res-option-value-of-learning

results.name: Livermore's trading maxims as Bellman value comparisons
results.status_text: conditional on the claim, which the chapter asserts by an appeal to Bayes' theorem and does not derive (it cites Polson and Witte 2014), that observing a loss lowers the value of the long action below the value of the neutral action, and, for never average down, that no outside information beyond what the market revealed has arrived
results.conditions: the claim, which the chapter asserts by an appeal to Bayes' theorem and does not derive (it cites Polson and Witte 2014), that observing a loss lowers the value of the long action below the value of the neutral action, and, for never average down, that no outside information beyond what the market revealed has arrived
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson and Witte (2014), A Bellman View of Jesse Livermore, arXiv:1407.2642.
results.summary: Livermore's maxims to cut losses and never average down are read as inequalities between Bellman action values after Bayesian updating of beliefs.
results.statement: In a Bellman (dynamic programming) formulation of a trading problem, let $Q_t(s,a)$ be the value of taking action $a$ in state $s$ at time $t$, with $a_L$ the long action and $a_N$ the neutral action. Suppose an investor holds a long position because $Q_t(s,a_L) > Q_t(s,a_N)$. If the position subsequently loses money, the price movement $x_t$ itself carries information, and by Bayes' theorem observing the loss should update beliefs to $q \cup \{x_t\}$ such that $Q_{t+1}^{q \cup \{x_t\}}(s',a_L) < Q_{t+1}^{q \cup \{x_t\}}(s',a_N)$, so that the optimal action is to exit; this is the chapter's reading of Livermore's maxim that profits always take care of themselves but losses never do. Averaging down would require $Q_t(s',a_L) > Q_t(s',a_N)$ after a loss, which, once beliefs are updated on the adverse price movement, typically cannot hold unless external information beyond what the market revealed has been received; this is the chapter's reading of Livermore's maxim never to average down.
results.label: res-livermore-maxims

results.name: Polya Gamma integral identity for binomial likelihoods
results.status_text: conditional on the identity and the conditional Polya Gamma law, which the chapter cites from Polson, Scott and Windle (2013) and does not prove
results.conditions: the identity and the conditional Polya Gamma law, which the chapter cites from Polson, Scott and Windle (2013) and does not prove
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson, Scott and Windle (2013), Bayesian Inference for Logistic Models Using Pólya Gamma Latent Variables, Journal of the American Statistical Association 108(504), 1339 to 1349.
results.summary: A binomial likelihood term in the linear predictor equals an exponential factor times a mixture of Gaussian kernels over a Polya Gamma variable, whose conditional law given the linear predictor is again Polya Gamma.
results.statement: Let $\mathrm{PG}(b,c)$, for $b>0$ and $c\in\mathbb{R}$, be the Polya Gamma distribution, the law of $X \stackrel{d}{=} \frac{1}{2\pi^2}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{g_k}{(k-1/2)^2 + c^2/(4\pi^2)}$, where the $g_k$ are independent $\mathrm{Ga}(b,1)$ gamma random variables. For $b>0$ and $a\in\mathbb{R}$, and for real $\psi$, the identity $\frac{(e^{\psi})^{a}}{(1+e^{\psi})^{b}} = 2^{-b} e^{\kappa\psi} \int_0^{\infty} e^{-\omega\psi^2/2}\, p(\omega)\, d\omega$ holds, where $\kappa = a - b/2$ and $p(\omega)$ is the density of $\omega \sim \mathrm{PG}(b,0)$. Moreover, the conditional distribution $p(\omega\mid\psi)$, with density proportional to $e^{-\omega\psi^2/2}p(\omega)$, is also in the Polya Gamma class: $(\omega\mid\psi) \sim \mathrm{PG}(b,\psi)$.
results.label: res-polya-gamma-identity

results.name: Polya Gamma Gibbs sampler for Bayesian logistic regression
results.status_text: conditional on the two conditional distributions, which the chapter quotes from Polson, Scott and Windle (2013) and does not derive from the integral identity, itself stated without proof
results.conditions: the two conditional distributions, which the chapter quotes from Polson, Scott and Windle (2013) and does not derive from the integral identity, itself stated without proof
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson, Scott and Windle (2013), Bayesian Inference for Logistic Models Using Pólya Gamma Latent Variables, Journal of the American Statistical Association 108(504), 1339 to 1349.
results.summary: For binomial logistic regression with a Gaussian prior, alternating a Polya Gamma draw of one latent variable per observation with a multivariate normal draw of the coefficients gives a two step Gibbs sampler.
results.statement: Let $\mathrm{PG}(h,c)$ denote the Polya Gamma distribution with parameters $h>0$ and $c\in\mathbb{R}$, the law of $\frac{1}{2\pi^2}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} g_k/((k-1/2)^2 + c^2/(4\pi^2))$ with the $g_k$ independent $\mathrm{Ga}(h,1)$. Suppose $y_i\mid\psi_i \sim \mathrm{Binom}(n_i, 1/(1+e^{-\psi_i}))$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$, where $\psi_i = x_i^\top\beta$, let $X$ be the design matrix with rows $x_i^\top$, let $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)$, and let the prior be $\beta \sim N(b,B)$ with mean vector $b$ and covariance matrix $B$. The Gibbs sampler iterates two steps. First, sample $(\omega_i\mid\beta) \sim \mathrm{PG}(n_i, x_i^\top\beta)$ for each observation. Second, sample $(\beta\mid y,\omega) \sim N(m_\omega, V_\omega)$, where $V_\omega = (X^\top\Omega X + B^{-1})^{-1}$, $m_\omega = V_\omega(X^\top\kappa + B^{-1}b)$, $\kappa = (y_1 - n_1/2, \ldots, y_n - n_n/2)$ and $\Omega = \mathrm{diag}(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_n)$.
results.label: res-polya-gamma-gibbs

results.name: Bartlett Fejer scale mixture representation of the exponential power prior
results.status_text: conditional on the representation, which the chapter states without proof and cites to Polson, Scott and Windle (2014), and an exponent in (0,1], so that the mixing weights are nonnegative
results.conditions: the representation, which the chapter states without proof and cites to Polson, Scott and Windle (2014), and an exponent in (0,1], so that the mixing weights are nonnegative
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson, Scott and Windle (2014), The Bayesian Bridge, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B 76(4), 713 to 733.
results.summary: The exponential power prior of the Bayesian bridge with exponent in (0,1] is a scale mixture of triangular Bartlett Fejer kernels with a two component gamma mixing distribution, stated in the chapter without proof and credited to Polson, Scott and Windle (2014).
results.statement: Let $\alpha \in (0,1]$ and $\tau > 0$, and let $p(\beta_j \mid \alpha, \tau) = \frac{1}{2\tau\Gamma(1+1/\alpha)} \exp\{-|\beta_j/\tau|^{\alpha}\}$ be the exponential power prior on a coefficient $\beta_j$. This prior is a scale mixture of triangular (Bartlett Fejer) kernels: given a mixing variable $\omega_j$, $p(\beta_j \mid \tau, \omega_j, \alpha) = \frac{1}{\tau \omega_j^{1/\alpha}} \left\{ 1 - \left| \frac{\beta_j}{\tau \omega_j^{1/\alpha}} \right| \right\}_+$, where $\{a\}_+ = \max(a,0)$, and $\omega_j \mid \alpha$ has the two component gamma mixture distribution $\frac{1+\alpha}{2} \,\mathrm{Gamma}(2+1/\alpha, 1) + \frac{1-\alpha}{2} \,\mathrm{Gamma}(1+1/\alpha, 1)$, where $\mathrm{Gamma}(a,1)$ is the gamma distribution with shape $a$ and unit scale. The restriction $\alpha \in (0,1]$ is what makes the mixture weights $(1 \pm \alpha)/2$ nonnegative.
results.label: res-bartlett-fejer-mixture

results.name: Posterior concentration at the minimax rate for sparse deep learning
results.status_text: conditional on the smoothness and prior mass conditions of Polson and Ročková (2018), which the chapter does not state, and the result itself, which it cites without proof; the minimax rate is for Hölder smooth regression functions on the unit cube
results.conditions: the smoothness and prior mass conditions of Polson and Ročková (2018), which the chapter does not state, and the result itself, which it cites without proof; the minimax rate is for Hölder smooth regression functions on the unit cube
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson and Ročková (2018), Posterior Concentration for Sparse Deep Learning, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 31, arXiv:1803.09138.
results.summary: Under smoothness and prior mass conditions, the posterior distribution of the regression function concentrates around the true function at the minimax rate, up to a factor of log N.
results.statement: Consider nonparametric regression $y_i = f(x_i) + \epsilon_i$ with $x_i = (x_{1i},\ldots,x_{di}) \in [0,1]^d$ and $N$ observations, and let $\hat f_N$ be the regularized MAP (maximum a posteriori) estimator $\hat f_N = \arg\min_{\hat f} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (y_i - \hat f(x_i))^2 + \phi(\hat f)$, where $\phi$ is a regularization term. Under smoothness and prior mass conditions, the posterior distribution $\Pi(f \mid x, y)$ concentrates around the true function at the minimax rate, up to a factor of $\log N$. Here, under standard assumptions, the minimax rate over Hölder smooth functions $f$ of order $\beta$ is of order $N^{-2\beta/(2\beta+d)}$ for the risk $R(f,\hat f_N) = \mathbb{E}_{X,Y}\|f-\hat f_N\|^2$, where $\|\cdot\|$ is the $L^2(P_X)$ norm.
results.label: res-posterior-concentration

results.name: Maximum expected utility by a quantile neural network
results.status_text: conditional on a known utility function, the ability to simulate parameters from the prior and data from the likelihood or a forward simulator, and a network that represents the quantile function of the utility; the chapter proves no approximation error, convergence rate or consistency result for the network
results.conditions: a known utility function, the ability to simulate parameters from the prior and data from the likelihood or a forward simulator, and a network that represents the quantile function of the utility; the chapter proves no approximation error, convergence rate or consistency result for the network
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson, Ruggeri and Sokolov (2024), Generative Bayesian Computation for Maximum Expected Utility, Entropy 26(12), 1076.
results.summary: A network trained with the check loss on simulated utilities, with the decision and the quantile level as inputs, approximates the quantile function of the utility; integrating it over the level approximates the expected utility, and the optimal decision maximizes that integral.
results.statement: Let $U(d,\theta)$ be a known utility of a decision $d$ and a parameter vector $\theta$, and let $S(y)$ be a statistic of the data $y$. Simulate prior and data pairs $(\theta^{(i)},y^{(i)})$, choose decisions $d_i$ independently of those pairs over the range of interest, draw independent levels $\tau_i\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$, and train a network $q_\varphi$ by minimizing $L(\varphi)=\frac1M\sum_{i=1}^M\rho_{\tau_i}\big(U(d_i,\theta^{(i)})-q_\varphi(S(y^{(i)}),d_i,\tau_i)\big)$, where $\rho_\tau$ is the check loss and $M$ counts training tuples. Given sufficient summaries and a successful fit, $q_\varphi(S(y),d,\tau)$ approximates the quantile function $F^{-1}_{U\mid d,y}(\tau)$, so the expected utility is approximately $\int_0^1 q_\varphi(S(y),d,\tau)\,d\tau$ and $d^\star(y)\approx\arg\max_d\int_0^1 q_\varphi(S(y),d,\tau)\,d\tau$. Because $d$ is an input, one network serves all decisions.
results.label: res-meu-quantile-network

results.name: Hierarchical model for second order trend filtering with quantile loss
results.status_text: conditional on the hierarchical representation, which the chapter attributes to Polson and Scott (2016) through envelope duality and does not derive, with unit likelihood scale and unpenalized level and slope, the conditions the chapter states for the posterior mode to give the penalized objective
results.conditions: the hierarchical representation, which the chapter attributes to Polson and Scott (2016) through envelope duality and does not derive, with unit likelihood scale and unpenalized level and slope, the conditions the chapter states for the posterior mode to give the penalized objective
results.origin_text: First stated in Polson and Scott (2016), Mixtures, Envelopes and Hierarchical Duality, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B 78(4), 701 to 727.
results.summary: Second order trend filtering with quantile loss has a working hierarchical model, an asymmetric Laplace likelihood with Laplace priors on second differences, whose posterior mode is the penalized estimate.
results.statement: Let $x_1<\dots<x_n$ be ordered inputs with responses $y_i$, let $\rho_\tau$ be the check loss at level $\tau$ and $\Delta^k$ the $k$th finite difference operator. Quantile trend filtering estimates $f$ by solving $\min_f\sum_{i=1}^n\rho_\tau(y_i-f(x_i))+\lambda\sum_{i=1}^{n-k}|\Delta^k f_i|$. For $k=2$, an asymmetric Laplace working likelihood $y_i\sim\mathrm{AsymmetricLaplace}(f_i,\tau,1)$ and Laplace priors $\Delta^2 f_i\sim\mathrm{Laplace}(0,1/\lambda)$, $i=2,\dots,n-1$, connect the penalized objective with a posterior mode: the asymmetric Laplace negative log likelihood is the check loss up to scale and constants, so with unpenalized level and slope the posterior mode gives the penalized estimate. This is a computational representation, not a claim that the errors follow that distribution.
results.label: res-quantile-trend-filtering
